newsitem.title: GERMANY: German firms seen unharmed by 1997 wage deals.
newsitem.headline: German firms seen unharmed by 1997 wage deals.

text.p: German companies, despite suffering an acutely embarrassing defeat in their attempts to implement a law cutting sick pay, are emerging with 1997 pay deals they can be happy with, economists said on Thursday.

Wage agreements in a number of industry sectors have now been reached after crisis negotiations that followed the introduction in October of a deeply unpopular law cutting sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.

Protests from workers in the metal and engineering, chemical and banking industries have led to many employers backing down on the cuts, which were supposed to bring German industry some 12 billion marks of cost savings.

But economists said that in allowing trade unions to come away from negotiations with the trophy of full sick pay, they have in many cases been able to enforce moderate, largely inflation-based 1997 wage increases in return.
"Companies can live with this kind of package -- especially the large ones," Deutsche Bank economist Hans-Juergen Meltzer said.

Meltzer said that bringing the wage negotiations forward from early next year -- ostensibly to confront the sick pay dispute -- actually benefited employers in sectors such as the chemical and engineering industries.

"As far as the economy is concerned, it was a case of the earlier the better for the employers," he said, adding that expectations of an improvement in German business conditions next year would have pushed wage agreements upwards.
Earlier on Thursday, employers in the chemical sector said they had secured a pay deal that will give the some 590,000 workers in the west German industry a wage increase of 1.5 percent in 1997.

The accord is similar to regional packages that have now been agreed for the vast majority of German's some 3.2 million metal and eingeering workers, where a 1.5 percent pay increase is to be followed by a 2.5 percent rise in 1998.
"The agreement itself in the metal sector is very moderate and it extends over two years, giving employers some degree of cost stability," BHF Bank economist Uwe Angenendt said.
Angenendt said the metal wage agreements were acting as a signal to pay negotiators in other areas.

White-collar trade union DAG said on Thursday it would be going into discussions for the banking sector looking for a headline wage rise of just 1.7 to 1.8 percent -- again, not significantly higher than many 1997 inflation forecasts.

Angenendt said German industry's long-running argument that labour costs make it uncompetitive in world markets had been made less pressing by the recent fall of the mark against other currencies, thus making German exports more attractive.
He warned however that one problem facing firms now was the uncertainty surrounding a major tax reform scheduled by the Bonn government for 1999.

Angenendt said the main impact of the uncertainty would be to reduce German companies' desire to invest over the next few years -- a development that will do nothing to reduce Germany's post-unification record of four million jobless.
